questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: compute work as the dot product of force and displacement
questions.stem: Ticket QA-4021 asks engineers to find the work done when a force of magnitude 5 newtons acts through a displacement of 4 meters at a 60 degree angle between them.

options.text: 10 joules, using the force magnitude times the displacement times the cosine
20 joules, from multiplying the two magnitudes without any angle factor
options.misconception: ignores the angle between the force and the displacement

options.text: 2.5 joules, from projecting the force but dropping the displacement length
options.misconception: drops the displacement length from the product

options.text: 5 joules, from multiplying the force by the cosine of the angle
options.misconception: forgets the displacement magnitude in the product

questions.explanation: Work is the dot product F·d = 5(4)cos60 degrees = 10 joules. Multiplying the magnitudes alone gives 20 joules, which wrongly assumes the force acts along the displacement.
questions.hint: Project the force onto the displacement direction first.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on a dot product
questions.learningObjective: bound a dot product with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
questions.stem: Ticket OPS-4402 asks whether the platform can promise a throughput estimate of 3000 units per second, noting the largest possible dot product for the two relevant vectors.

options.text: The dot product is at most the sum of the two vector magnitudes
options.misconception: adds the magnitudes instead of multiplying them

options.text: The dot product cannot exceed the product of the two vector magnitudes
The dot product is always less than the larger of the two magnitudes
options.misconception: confuses a bound with the value the dot product must take

options.text: The dot product is unbounded because the angle term can turn negative
options.misconception: overlooks that the cosine factor is bounded by one

questions.explanation: Cauchy-Schwarz states that the absolute dot product is at most the product of the two magnitudes. Adding the magnitudes or dropping the cosine factor gives a bound that is not valid.
questions.hint: The tightest general bound multiplies the two magnitudes.

questions.stem: Ticket MAP-4017 gives two vectors, one of magnitude 9 and one of magnitude 6, meeting at an angle of 60 degrees, and asks the crew to report the scalar projection of the first onto the second.
questions.explanation: The scalar projection of u on v is the magnitude of u times the cosine of the angle, so 9 times 0.5 gives 4.5. Multiplying the two magnitudes, 54, ignores the angle entirely.
questions.hint: Multiply the source magnitude by the cosine of the angle.

options.misconception: ignores the tilt of the force arrow in the diagram

A horizontal arrow of length 30 newtons from adding the two components
options.misconception: adds perpendicular components that do not align

questions.explanation: The projection of the 20 newton force onto the horizontal direction is 20 cos 30 degrees, about 17.3 newtons. The sine gives the vertical component, not the horizontal push.

questions.learningObjective: identify the perpendicular remainder left by a projection

options.text: The remainder, which is the same direction as the original vector
options.misconception: confuses the remainder with the original vector

options.text: The remainder, which is perpendicular to the vector being projected onto
options.misconception: states the wrong perpendicular direction in the explanation

options.misconception: believes the decomposition has only one piece

options.text: The remainder, which is perpendicular to the target and shorter than the input

questions.topic: Cyclic order of unit vector products
questions.learningObjective: apply the cyclic order of the standard unit vector products
questions.stem: Ticket CONV-4007 asks which sequence of unit vector cross products keeps the right-hand rule orientation when the basis is standard.

options.text: i cross j equals k, j cross k equals i, and k cross i equals j
i cross j equals k, j cross k equals i, and i cross k equals j
options.misconception: reverses the last cyclic pair and breaks the right-hand rule

options.text: i cross j equals k, k cross j equals i, and j cross i equals k
options.misconception: swaps an order and flips the sign of a cyclic product

options.text: i cross j equals k, j cross k equals i, and i cross j equals i
options.misconception: repeats the first pair and never reaches the last one

questions.explanation: The cyclic order i cross j = k, j cross k = i, k cross i = j is the standard right-handed basis. Reversing any single pair flips the sign of that product and breaks the cyclic pattern.
questions.hint: Move the last unit vector to the front to continue.

options.text: Point it in the direction the first vector turns toward the second
options.misconception: reverses the right-hand rule by swapping the two vectors

options.text: Point it using the right-hand rule, curling from the first to the second
Point it along the sum of the two vectors to keep it between them
options.misconception: believes the cross product lies in the plane of its inputs

options.text: Point it along the difference of the two vectors to face the smaller angle
options.misconception: uses a vector difference that describes no real direction

questions.explanation: The cross product of two nonparallel vectors is perpendicular to both, and the right-hand rule fixes which way it points. Summing the inputs would give a vector inside their plane.

questions.topic: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on a dot product
questions.learningObjective: identify when the Cauchy-Schwarz bound is attained
questions.stem: Ticket SCHED-4010 claims two vectors can attain the largest possible dot product, and asks when the bound is actually reached.

options.text: Only when one of the vectors is the zero vector
options.misconception: thinks equality needs a zero vector, not parallel vectors

options.text: Only when the two vectors point in opposite directions
options.misconception: believes the cosine must be negative to reach the bound

options.text: Only when the two vectors are parallel and point the same way
Only when the two vectors are perpendicular to each other
options.misconception: confuses the maximizing angle with a right angle

questions.explanation: Equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz bound holds when the vectors are parallel and the cosine of the angle between them is 1. Perpendicular vectors give a dot product of zero, the opposite extreme.
questions.hint: The cosine factor must reach its largest value.

questions.learningObjective: locate a lost minus sign in a determinant expansion
questions.stem: Ticket REVIEW-4014 says a colleague expanded the cross product determinant and produced a negative y component, asking which sign convention was dropped.

options.text: The sign was dropped because the determinant row was written upward
options.misconception: blames the row order instead of the missing minus sign

options.text: The minus sign on the second determinant term was lost in the expansion
The sign was dropped because the cross product order was reversed
options.misconception: claims the vector order changed, flipping every sign

options.text: The sign was dropped because a zero component was assumed
options.misconception: invents a zero component to explain a sign change

questions.explanation: In the standard expansion the second and third terms carry explicit minus signs, so dropping one flips a single coordinate. Reversing the input order would flip all three coordinates at once.

questions.explanation: Work equals 9 times 6 times cos 60 degrees, which is 27 joules. The same product without the angle factor would be 54 joules, overstating the contribution.
questions.hint: Work is the dot product of force and displacement.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Cauchy-Schwarz bound on a dot product
questions.learningObjective: compute the sharp bound for a dot product
questions.stem: Ticket CAP-4034 needs an upper limit on a dot product of vectors with magnitudes 6 and 9 and asks for the best general guarantee.

options.text: The dot product is at most 15, the sum of the two magnitudes
options.misconception: adds the magnitudes instead of multiplying them

options.text: The dot product is at most 3, the difference of the two magnitudes
options.misconception: subtracts the magnitudes to build a bound

options.text: The dot product is at most 54, the product of the two magnitudes
The dot product is at most 81, the square of the larger magnitude
options.misconception: squares a magnitude and ignores the other vector

questions.explanation: Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the dot product by the product of the magnitudes, 6 times 9 giving 54, and this bound is sharp when the vectors are parallel. Sums and squares give no valid guarantee.
questions.hint: Multiply the magnitudes to get the sharp bound.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: predict the effect of using a unit target vector
questions.stem: Ticket VEC-4035 asks how the scalar projection changes when the target vector is replaced by its unit vector along the same direction.

options.text: It grows by the length of the original target vector
options.misconception: scales the projection up instead of leaving it alone

options.text: It shrinks to the reciprocal of the target magnitude
options.misconception: invents a reciprocal rule for the target length

options.text: It becomes the dot product of the two original vectors
options.misconception: switches the operation to the dot product

options.text: It stays the same, because the angle and the source length are unchanged

questions.explanation: The scalar projection depends only on the direction of the target, since it uses the cosine of the angle. Replacing the target by its unit vector keeps that direction and therefore the same value.
questions.hint: The scalar projection only uses direction.

questions.explanation: The component along the surface is 20 cos 60 degrees, which is 10 newtons. The perpendicular component would be 20 sin 60 degrees, a different quantity from the one asked for.

questions.learningObjective: state the existence and uniqueness of a projection split
questions.stem: Ticket CLEAN-4037 asks what should be said about splitting a vector into a parallel part and a perpendicular part.

options.text: The split always exists and is unique for a fixed target direction
The split exists only when the two parts have the same length
options.misconception: adds a condition that is not needed for the split

options.text: The split may be chosen freely, since many decompositions work
options.misconception: claims a non-unique decomposition where there is only one

options.text: The split fails when the source is shorter than the target
options.misconception: ties existence to comparing two magnitudes

questions.explanation: Every vector splits uniquely into the component along a fixed target direction and the leftover perpendicular to it. Nothing about the relative lengths of the two vectors can prevent that split.
questions.hint: Projection onto a direction is always well defined.

questions.topic: Cross product by the determinant rule
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a zero cross product for nonparallel vectors
questions.stem: Ticket RENDER-4038 reports a cross product of the zero vector for two clearly nonparallel input vectors, and asks what mistake was made.

options.text: The magnitudes were divided instead of multiplied in the components
options.misconception: blames a scaling slip that would not zero the result

options.text: The vectors were treated as parallel, so a zero result was assumed
The cross product was computed with the inputs in the wrong order
options.misconception: claims an ordering slip produces a zero vector

options.text: The determinant was expanded along the wrong row of the matrix
options.misconception: blames the expansion row for a zero outcome

questions.explanation: The cross product vanishes only for parallel inputs. Reordering the inputs negates the result but never annihilates it.
questions.hint: When is the cross product exactly zero?

options.misconception: takes the cross product along one of its inputs

options.text: Straight right, continuing the direction of the first arrow
options.misconception: takes the cross product along the other input arrow

Along the diagonal between the two drawn arrows
options.misconception: places the cross product inside the plane of the arrows

questions.explanation: Rotating from the first arrow to the second through the smaller angle gives an out-of-page direction by the right-hand rule. The cross product is perpendicular to the page, never along either arrow.

options.text: The displacement alone, since the force only sets the scale
options.misconception: claims force does not affect the product

options.text: Either one, since the two quantities multiply to the same result
options.misconception: treats the product as independent of its factors

options.text: The product of the two magnitudes, which is the work when aligned

questions.explanation: When the force and displacement are aligned, the cosine is one and the work equals the product of the magnitudes. The two factors still play different roles, so neither quantity alone equals the work.
questions.hint: Aligned vectors make the cosine equal to one.

The scalar projection of u on v uses the magnitude of v and the angle to u

options.misconception: drops the cosine factor and keeps only the product

options.text: The scalar projection of u on v uses the magnitude of the larger vector only
options.misconception: ignores the angle and the smaller vector

questions.explanation: The projection of u onto v has length equal to the magnitude of u times the cosine of the angle, so the source supplies the magnitude and the target only sets the direction.

The height on the wall, which is the other component of the ladder

options.text: The length times the sine of the angle the ladder makes with the floor
options.misconception: uses the sine for an along-the-floor component

questions.learningObjective: relate the determinant rule to the size of a cross product
questions.stem: Ticket RENDER-4046 asks a team to relate the determinant rule to the size of the cross product.

options.text: The determinant gives the cross product length directly as a number
options.misconception: confuses the determinant with the magnitude

options.text: The determinant gives the area times the length of the longer vector
options.misconception: invents a mixed area and length formula

options.text: The determinant gives the three components, and their norm is the magnitude
The determinant gives the angle between the vectors, and nothing else
options.misconception: claims the output is an angle rather than a vector

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because the dot product always equals that product
options.misconception: assumes the bound is always attained exactly

options.text: The claim is wrong, because the dot product can be smaller than the product
Nothing is wrong, because the angle factor can only be positive
options.misconception: overlooks that the angle may exceed ninety degrees

options.text: The claim is wrong, because the bound needs a sum instead of a product
options.misconception: replaces the correct product bound with a sum

questions.explanation: Cauchy-Schwarz gives an upper bound of 3 times 8, which is 24, not a lower bound, and the dot product reaches zero for perpendicular vectors. The angle factor can also make the dot product negative.
